name: Gua Metanduno
charac_lvl1: Rock art site / Petroglyph / Pictograph / Hand stencil
comments: The rock paintings are generally still visible, notwithstanding some vandalism on the left wall and inside the cave. Some of the paintings are covered with green lichen and some of the images are peeling away from the wall. Most of the paintings are in the cave's well-lit zone. Kosasih (1985) originally recorded 316 paintings at this site. The painted motifs include a wide variety of human figures, horses, deer, pigs, dogs, chickens, snakes, centipedes, boats, sun figures, hand stencils, and unidentifiable motifs (Figure 6.8). The large corpus of work was created mainly using brown and red ochre, along with charcoal for the black figures. The painting techniques used at the site consisted of applying pigment directly to the walls producing solid stick figures, outlines and solid infill depictions of humans and animals, except for the hand stencils, which were made with sprayed pigment. One of the hand stencils can be found on the inside of the cave and another five at the right of the entrance, all of which were found later during the 2015 survey at the site. The Gua Metanduno human figures are depicted in a multitude of activities and dynamic actions, including mounted and unmounted hunters, humans in combat, humans with hands on their waist, flying humans, and apparently unfinished paintings. The cave paintings overall are dominated by horses, which probably arrived in Muna within the last 500 years or so (see Discussion). The rock art often features boats with passengers, perhaps suggesting inter-island voyaging for trade and/or combat.

name: Gua Toyapakeh
comments: Song Toyapakeh is a submerged cave located on Nusa Penida Island, Bali, at a depth of 16 m below sea level. The cave is believed to have been inhabited by human during the late Pleistocene period, as evidenced by the large numbers of bones from Cervidae and Elephantoid families, as well as turtles, that are scattered throughout the cave. The presence of these bones raises questions about the past use of Song Toyapakeh by humans and the transformation of the island's landscape into a submerged cave.

comments: Topogaro 2, part of the Goa Topogaro cave complex in Central Sulawesi, preserves deposits up to 3 m deep, with occupations dated from about 29 ka to the Metal Age. Excavations yielded lithic flakes of chert. Use-wear analysis indicates activities such as plant processing, bone working, and butchering. Occupation was episodic, with gaps during the LGM but renewed use in the Post-LGM, Holocene, and later periods.

comments: The Gua Jimbe site (Java) Ñ The fossils from the Gua Jimbe site have also been col- lected by Dubois in 1890. It is situated near Redjobangan, c. 10 km west of Blitar in East Java (van den Brink, 1983). There are only a few notes about this site and it is not possible to give a reconstruction of the site and the excavation. In August 1890 Dubois stated about the Gua Jimbe site that c. 2 m beneath the surface a carafe, thur- ible, simple earthenware lamp and some copper ornaments had been found. He mentioned that at a depth of at least 3 m bones of pig, muntjak, small cat, porcupine, and monkeys had been found. Furthermore, human remains (mandible, maxilla and postcranial material) had also been found at this level. I think that the layer of 3 m (where bone tools, human and faunal remains have been found) belongs to an older period than the layer at a depth of 2 m. Data considering the fauna from this site have been published by Brongersma (1941), Hooijer (1946, 1962) and have been described by van den Brink (1983). Fragments of the human remains have been described by Nelson (1988,1989).

name: Trinil
comments: Description: In the 1890s, a young military doctor named Eugene Dubois, assigned two officers of KNIL, Corporal Anthonie de Winter and Gerardus Kriele, to collect fossils from the Kendeng hills. Between 1891-1894 Dubois led the research in Trinil, finding a calotte, femur, and teeth assigned to Pithecanthropus erectus (now Homo erectus) (Dubois 1894). After Kriel and de Winter finished his excavations at Trinil, from 1906-1908 the fieldwork to search for more new Pithecanthropus bone was continued by Lenore Selenka near the location of Dubois' excavation (Selenka and Blanckenhorn 1911). Although the Selenka expedition did not find new hominin remains, it yielded important contextual data through systematic and multidisciplinary approaches. Recent analysis on the Dubois' collection by Joordens et al. (2015) found geometric pattern on the Pseudodon shell claimed from the same layer of Pithecanthropus erectus. The Dubois' description on Trinil specimens is the reference (holotype) for the species of Homo erectus.

name: Makpan Cave
charac_lvl1: Shell midden / Shell mound / Bukit Kerang / Kjokkenmoddinger
comments: "" ""Description: Makpan is a large lava tube cave on the southwest coast of Alor that dates first occupation to ~39,500 +/- 500 years ago. The cave entrance faces the ocean and today it is ~386 m from the shoreline and ~37.5 m above current mean sea level. As on the north coast of Timor, the offshore topography in this region drops away steeply to a depth of 100 m, less than 1.8 km off the current shoreline so Makpan would have not been much further from the coast when first occupied ~40,000 years ago. The 2016 excavation produced a remarkably rich assemblage comprised predominately of marine resources, including fish, shellfish and sea urchins. The initial phase of occupation at Makpan from ~40,000 until 22,000 is marked by relatively low-density bone and shell accumulations suggesting that occupation was limited and sporadic early on. Marine fauna dominates the subsistence resources in this level with a focus on urchin exploitation. This was followed by a terminal Pleistocene phase showing an increase in occupation intensity beginning ~14,000 years ago. The densest phase of occupation is marked by the deposition of a dense shell midden and marine fauna during the Pleistocene-Holocene transition beginning ~12,000 years ago. The site appears to have been little used from ~7000 until 3500 years ago when the Neolithic to historic occupation begins. In this upper level marine resource use continues and pottery and domestic animals appear in the assemblage. Makpan contained a remarkably rich assemblage of shellfish hooks and beads dating from ~15,000 years ago. The lithic assemblages included fine and course grade volcanic flakes and cores with a small assemblage of chert and obsidian. Unlike nearby Tron Bon Lei, most of the obsidian artefacts are probably derived from local sources. A number of grindstones were also recovered from Makpan including a basalt muller with a polished surface from the initial occupation phase, and a grindstone from the terminal Pleistocene with red staining, possibly from grinding ochre. name: Ngandong
comments: Description: Ngandong is one of the most important Homo erectus sites in Java, located on the Solo River. The site has yielded a series of fossil hominid remains dating to 117,000-108,000 years ago, representing the last known appearance of Homo erectus in Java. Over 20 cranial specimens and thousands of vertebrate fossils have been found at this site.

name: Gua Golo
bibliography: Bellwood, P. (1997). The Spice Islands in Prehistory: Archaeology in the Northern Moluccas, Indonesia. Canberra: Terra Australis 24, ANU.
comments: Description: Gua Golo is a Neolithic site on Gebe Island in the Northern Moluccas. The cave contains evidence of early Austronesian migration through Wallacea, with finds including Tridacna shell adzes and pottery. The site is significant for understanding the spread of Austronesian-speaking peoples through eastern Indonesia.

name: Calio
comments: Description: Calio is an Early Pleistocene site in Sulawesi where stone tools dating to approximately 1.04 million years ago were discovered. This represents the earliest evidence of hominins on Sulawesi and demonstrates that early humans crossed ocean barriers to reach isolated islands in Wallacea much earlier than previously thought.

name: Samblingan
comments: Description: Sambungmacan (also spelled Sambingan) is an open site on the south bank of the Solo River in central Java. Several Homo erectus crania have been found here, including Sambungmacan 1, 3, and 4. The fossils date to the late Middle Pleistocene and are important for understanding the evolution of Homo erectus in Java.

name: Madura Strait
comments: Description: The Madura Strait fossil assemblage was discovered during dredging operations in the Java Sea. Two Homo erectus skull fragments were found, dating to approximately 140,000 years ago. This submerged site represents a Late Pleistocene river valley system that was exposed during lower sea levels. The fossils provide unique insights into Homo erectus behavior, including selective hunting and marrow processing.

name: Mojokerto (Perning)
comments: Description: The Mojokerto (Perning) site in East Java is famous for the discovery of Mojokerto 1, a Homo erectus cranial vault found in 1936. The site is located near Perning village, Mojokerto Regency. Recent dating suggests an age of approximately 1.8-1.7 million years old, making it one of the oldest Homo erectus specimens in Java.

name: Patiayam
comments: Description: Patiayam is an important fossil site in Kudus Regency, Central Java, part of the Patiayam Dome on the Muria Mountain slope. The site has yielded numerous Pleistocene fossils including Stegodon, giant tortoise, and other megafauna. Associated with the Northern zone of Java Homo erectus sites.

name: Ngawi
comments: Description: Ngawi is a Homo erectus site in Ngawi Regency, East Java. The site yielded the Ngawi 1 calvaria, an important fossil specimen for understanding Homo erectus evolution in Java. Located in the Solo River basin area.

name: Lida Ajer
comments: Description: Lida Ajer is a cave in West Sumatra containing early modern human remains. Two modern human teeth were discovered, dating to approximately 73,000-63,000 years ago, making it one of the oldest confirmed modern human occupations in island Southeast Asia. The site was first investigated by Eugene Dubois in the late 19th century and rediscovered in recent years.

name: Kedungbrubus
comments: Description: Kedungbrubus is a Homo erectus site in Madiun Regency, East Java, located in the Kendeng area. The site is part of the classic Java hominid-bearing succession along with Trinil, Sangiran, and others. The site has yielded fossil remains of Homo erectus and associated fauna.

name: Song Tritis
comments: Description: Song Tritis is a cave in the Gunungsewu karst region, Gunungkidul, Yogyakarta. Archaeological excavations have revealed human skeletal remains dating to approximately 4,500 years ago, as well as pottery evidence indicating sustained occupation during the mid-Holocene period.

name: Sukajadi
charac_lvl1: Shell midden / Shell mound / Bukit Kerang / Kjokkenmoddinger
comments: Description: Sukajadi (Sukajadi Pasar) is a shell midden site in northern Sumatra, part of the Bukit Kerang tradition. The site contains evidence of early Holocene occupation with marine shell deposits and is associated with early Homo sapiens in the region. Similar to other Bukit Kerang sites in Aceh Tamiang.

name: Tamiang
charac_lvl1: Shell midden / Shell mound / Bukit Kerang / Kjokkenmoddinger
comments: Description: Tamiang (Bukit Kerang) is a shell midden site in Aceh Tamiang Regency, Aceh. The site is part of the widespread Bukit Kerang tradition of prehistoric hunter-gatherer sites in northern Sumatra, dating to the Holocene period. Shell deposits indicate marine resource exploitation by early coastal communities.
